items.title: Happy birthday, Chris Watson, co-founder of Cabaret Voltaire
items.summary: Chris Watson, co-founder of Cabaret Voltaire, turns 73 on 21 November 2026. A look at his industrial music years and his field recording career since.
items.fullText:
Chris Watson, co-founder of Sheffield industrial group Cabaret Voltaire, turns 73 on 21 November 2026. Watson helped shape the band’s early, abrasive sound before leaving in 1981 to build an internationally recognised career in field recording and wildlife sound, work that has since earned him three BAFTA awards for Best Factual Sound.

Today we celebrate Chris Watson, one of the founding figures of British industrial music and an artist whose career has taken him from the experimental electronic underground of Sheffield to some of the most remote acoustic environments on Earth.

In 1973, Watson co-founded Cabaret Voltaire with Richard H. Kirk and Stephen Mallinder. Using tape loops, found sounds, primitive electronics and manipulated recordings, the trio challenged conventional ideas of composition, rhythm and instrumentation and developed an abrasive, often unsettling language that became fundamental to the emergence of industrial music. Early releases such as “Mix-Up” (1979), “The Voice of America” (1980) and “Red Mecca” (1981) remain key documents of a period when electronic experimentation was becoming inseparable from the political and cultural tensions of post-industrial Britain.

After leaving Cabaret Voltaire in 1981, Watson joined Tyne Tees Television and continued his sound experiments through The Hafler Trio, formed with Andrew M. McKenzie, before developing an extraordinary career in wildlife and environmental recording. His subsequent work for television, radio and documentary productions, including BBC natural history programmes with Sir David Attenborough, allowed him to pursue an interest that had been present since his earliest experiments with tape: the possibility of discovering musical structures within sounds that already exist around us. That work has brought him three BAFTA awards for Best Factual Sound, for “The Life of Birds” (1998), “Frozen Planet” (2012) and “The Secret World of Sound with David Attenborough” (2025).

His solo recordings, including “Stepping into the Dark” (1996), “Weather Report” (2003) and “El Tren Fantasma” (2011), demonstrate an exceptional sensitivity to acoustic detail, duration and the spatial character of sound. From the movement of glaciers and the calls of wildlife to the mechanical rhythms of a train crossing Mexico, Watson builds sonic narratives from these recordings without relying on conventional musical instrumentation. Careful editing and composition give these recordings relationships between sounds that a casual listen would miss.

2026 has been another busy year in Watson’s career. Following Cabaret Voltaire’s 50th-anniversary return to the stage in 2025, he and Stephen Mallinder embarked on farewell performances celebrating the group’s legacy and their late collaborator Richard H. Kirk, who died in 2021. Watson also released “Planet Ocean” through Touch, an album of recordings devoted to the rhythms, textures and acoustic life of the world’s oceans.

Watson’s artistic journey ties these different worlds together. The musician who once experimented with tape manipulation and electronic noise in Sheffield has spent decades investigating the equally complex sonic structures of nature, applying the same curiosity and attention to sounds that conventional listening frequently overlooks.

Happy birthday, Chris Watson. Thank you for an extraordinary contribution to industrial and experimental music, for the pioneering work of Cabaret Voltaire, and for decades of recordings that have expanded what sound, and listening itself, can reveal.

About Chris Watson

Chris Watson was born on 21 November 1953 in the Sheffield suburb of Totley, England. He is a musician, sound artist and field recordist whose career spans both experimental electronic music and contemporary sound art. In 1973 he co-founded the pioneering industrial group Cabaret Voltaire alongside Richard H. Kirk and Stephen Mallinder. His early experiments with tape manipulation, found sounds and electronics on albums including “Mix-Up”, “The Voice of America” and “Red Mecca” contributed to a musical language that went on to influence generations of industrial, post-punk and electronic artists.

Following his departure from Cabaret Voltaire in October 1981, Watson joined Tyne Tees Television and formed The Hafler Trio with Andrew M. McKenzie before establishing himself as one of the world’s leading specialists in wildlife and environmental sound recording. His work has taken him across the globe, capturing the acoustic environments of remote landscapes, animal habitats and natural phenomena, and he has contributed to BBC natural history productions associated with Sir David Attenborough, including “The Life of Birds”, “Frozen Planet” and “The Secret World of Sound with David Attenborough”, which brought him BAFTA awards for Best Factual Sound in 1998, 2012 and 2025 respectively.

His solo releases on the Touch label include “Stepping into the Dark” (1996), “Outside the Circle of Fire” (1998), “Weather Report” (2003, named one of “1000 albums to hear before you die” by The Guardian in 2007), “El Tren Fantasma” (2011) and “Planet Ocean” (2026). Through these recordings, Watson transforms environmental sound into acoustic works that sit between music, documentary and sound art.

In May 2025, Watson and Mallinder announced they would reunite as Cabaret Voltaire for a 50th-anniversary performance at Sheffield’s Sensoria Festival, followed by a final tour and the live album “But What Time Is It Really?” through 2026, alongside an ongoing reissue campaign for “CODE” on Mute. Official website: chriswatson.net.

items.title: Toy Weather’s 1995 album ‘Seasons Of Fairytales’ gets a digital reissue via Sub Culture Records
items.summary: Toy Weather's 1995 album "Seasons Of Fairytales" is now a digital reissue via Sub Culture Records on Bandcamp, released November 20, 2026.
items.fullText:
More than three decades after its original release, Norwegian electronic project Toy Weather’s album Seasons Of Fairytales is getting another chance to be discovered. Sub Culture Records released the 14-track album digitally on November 20, 2026.

Originally released on CD in 1995, “Seasons Of Fairytales” was written and produced by Svein Hovland. The album draws on several musical styles, with elements of electronic music, art rock, progressive rock and darker, more experimental sounds.

The record moves between different musical approaches without sticking to one particular genre, reflecting a time when electronic music was exploring territory well beyond the dancefloor.

The album includes tracks such as “The Season Of Fairytales”, “Moods Like Jeans”, “The Better Of Mysteries”, “Shadow Pictures” and “Quiet On The Western Front”.

With this digital reissue, Sub Culture Records is bringing a piece of Norwegian electronic music history back into circulation. For those who remember the original CD, it is an opportunity to hear the album again. For everyone else, it is a chance to discover a recording that first appeared more than 30 years ago.

The full tracklist:

  1. The Season Of Fairytales
  2. Moods Like Jeans
  3. Move ‘Round
  4. Fire In Water
  5. The Better Of Mysteries
  6. Big View
  7. Shadow Pictures
  8. Do Or Die
  9. Kill My Dreams
  10. Rise & Fall
  11. Thresholds
  12. A Definition
  13. Quiet On The Western Front
  14. The Stranger Dance

About Toy Weather

Toy Weather is the recording project of Norwegian musician Svein Hovland. “Seasons Of Fairytales” first appeared on CD in 1995, before streaming and digital distribution gave older recordings this kind of second life.

Hovland kept releasing music as Toy Weather in the years since. In 2026, the project returned with the album “Feathers in a Strange Wind” on Apollon Records, with Hovland on vocals and guitar alongside Frank Hovland on bass and Rune Kogstad on drums, and a standalone single, “Woodstock Morning”. The reissue of “Seasons Of Fairytales” through Sub Culture Records gives listeners a way to hear where that sound started, three decades earlier.

items.title: Fear Maintenance releases ‘New Dawn Fades’ cover and video
items.summary: Solo project Fear Maintenance released a cover of Joy Division's "New Dawn Fades" with a self-made video on November 18, 2026, its third post-punk single.
items.fullText:
Burlington, Ontario solo project Fear Maintenance released a cover of Joy Division’s “New Dawn Fades” on November 18, 2026, its third single since musician Colin Adams began reworking post-punk songs under the name. The track is also available on Spotify and other streaming services.

Adams arranged, performed, produced, recorded, mixed and mastered the cover alone in his Burlington home studio over four months. He built the arrangement around the final minute of Joy Division’s original, extending the instrumental coda that follows Ian Curtis’s last line into what Adams calls a “sonic explosion,” describing it as the sound of someone in the middle of an emotional breakdown.

Adams also conceived, shot and edited the video himself, working with a green screen in a ten-by-eight-foot space in his basement over four months, usually shooting between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. He describes the approach as reflecting “the internal strife and self-loathing of the protagonist as he metaphorically beat himself up.”

“New Dawn Fades” is track five on Joy Division’s debut album “Unknown Pleasures,” released by Factory Records in June 1979 following sessions with producer Martin Hannett at Strawberry Studios in Stockport. An instrumental edit of a Moby cover of the song appeared in Michael Mann’s 1995 film “Heat.”

About Fear Maintenance

Fear Maintenance is the solo project of Colin Adams, a musician based in Burlington, Ontario, Canada, who plays, produces and records all of its material alone in his home studio. The project revisits post-punk songs from the late 1970s and 1980s that Adams says inspired him to become a musician, and has released no original material under the name.

Adams was fifteen when he joined the Toronto band Face of Another as guitarist in 1986. Its bassist, Tim Smith, introduced him to Joy Division; the two later fell out and never spoke again. After Smith’s death, Adams and his former bandmates revisited their old songs for Smith’s family, and on the second anniversary of Smith’s death, Adams recorded a cover of “Ceremony.” The recordings that followed became Fear Maintenance, a name Adams took from the label that released “I Live,” a 1995 EP by his second Toronto band, In Faith, which played Toronto clubs including Lee’s Palace from 1990 to 1995.

Adams opened the project with a cover of Depeche Mode’s “Stripped” in December 2025, followed by a cover of Joy Division’s “Shadowplay” released with a video on August 13, 2026. “New Dawn Fades” is the third single in the series.

items.title: KOSMOBERKH releases ‘Troglobiten in Absonderlicht’ album
items.summary: Hanover project KOSMOBERKH released "Troglobiten in Absonderlicht" on November 6, 2026, via Zeichenlos Records, its first album since 2018's "oneiroi."
items.fullText:
Hanover, Germany-based project KOSMOBERKH released “Troglobiten in Absonderlicht” on November 6, 2026, via Zeichenlos Records, the label founded by the project’s sole member, David Barteczko. The ten-track album is Barteczko’s first since 2018’s “oneiroi,” released under the project name Mosaikh.

The album’s title translates, in Barteczko’s own rendering, as “Troglobites in Secluded Light.” Acoustic guitar and cello, played by Jann Michael Engel, anchor the record, with synths, electronic percussion and field recordings extending the arrangements beyond their acoustic core. Bandcamp tags the album cinematic, dreamy and experimental, alongside Barteczko’s own term for his work, “singer-doomwriter.” Barteczko names early Dead Can Dance, Scott Walker’s “Scott 4,” David Bowie’s “The Man Who Sold the World” and Peter Hammill’s “In Camera” among his reference points.

Engel’s cello was recorded in Göttingen; Barteczko tracked his own vocals, synths, percussion and effects at home, and most of the guitars were recorded at Holodeck Studio, where Alex Pojda co-produced the album with Barteczko and handled mixing and mastering. Christoffer Grunau plays drums and Udo Kirfel contributes bass on “Telegramme,” and Christof Schlaak plays piano on the closing track, “Petrichor.”

The ten tracks are “Fiz Oblon,” “Asche meiner Jugend,” “Sterngeworden,” “Zugvogel,” “Hybris,” “Telegramme,” “Stummfilm,” “Zypressen,” “Oras Bad” and “Petrichor.” Four advance singles preceded the album: “Stummfilm” (August 14), “Zypressen” (September 4), “Petrichor” (September 25) and “Fiz Oblon” (October 16), each released with its own video.

The black gatefold vinyl edition is limited to 120 copies, and both the LP and the digital download are exclusive to Bandcamp. “Troglobiten in Absonderlicht” is also available on streaming services, including Spotify.

About KOSMOBERKH

KOSMOBERKH is the project of Hanover, Germany-based singer, guitarist and lyricist David Barteczko, who first performed the material on an open stage at Craftwork Café in Oldenburg between 2011 and 2013. The 2014 demo “Urbild” began his recording partnership with Alex Pojda. Barteczko set aside vocals for the instrumental post-rock of “Dim Nachttag” in 2016, then took up singing again on 2018’s “oneiroi,” released under the project name Mosaikh as an electric trio.

During a break from KOSMOBERKH, Barteczko played in the prog-doom band CMDR RIKR and the post-rock group BRUECKEN. He returned to the stage in May 2024, opening for Extra Life at Cadillac in Oldenburg alongside cellist Jann Michael Engel, whose own credits include work with Anne Clark and Mila Mar. “Troglobiten in Absonderlicht” is KOSMOBERKH’s first album since that return, and the first released on Barteczko’s own label, Zeichenlos Records.

items.title: Kontrast – Imperium – Proteus (Digital/Vinyl Album – Danse Macabre Records)
items.summary: The German band Kontrast has been active for some 30 years and boasts an extensive...
items.fullText:
The German band Kontrast has been active for some 30 years and boasts an extensive discography, including a nearly 20-year relationship with Danse Macabre Records. With “Imperium – Proteus”, they complete the two-part album series that began last year with the highly commendable “Imperium – Tyrannis”. Like its predecessor, this album contains 10 tracks. It is also worth noting that both albums are available together as a single CD package.

Upon exploring this release, one immediately notices a distinct difference compared to its predecessor, which, to my ears, sounded harder and was more deeply rooted in an EBM aesthetic. These new tracks lean more towards Electro-Pop, at times even bordering on Future-Pop. Above all, this is an incredibly varied, Pop-oriented record. Its vintage textures occasionally evoke the magic of Welle:Erdball, while other tracks feature harsher arrangements like a wink to Das Ich. The album is primarily danceable, although it also offers a few quieter, more subdued moments. The inclusion of both male and female vocals further enhances the diversity of the overall sound.

Personally, I find the first instalment of the “Imperium” series slightly stronger, but this follow-up certainly has plenty to offer as well. Perhaps the best option is to pick up the CD edition, which brings both releases together in one package. (Rating:7½).

Listen to “Cassettenmensch”:

About Kontrast

The German band Kontrast formed in Germany in 1992, when Dirk Heinrich, Roberto Lindner and Tobias Messias founded the project under the name ISECS; Falko Heinbokel joined in 1995. An early demo of “Einheitsschritt” (“Drei Schritte vor und drei zurück”) appeared in 1994 and grew into an independent-scene anthem by 1996. The band adopted the name Kontrast in 1999, debuting under it that May in support of Clan of Xymox.

Kontrast’s first album, “Programm”, followed in 2002 on the UpSolution label; Danse Macabre Records reissued it as a 20th-anniversary “Programm: Deluxe Edition” in 2022, which reached number two on the Deutsche Alternative Charts and was reviewed by Side-Line. A second album, “Industrie<>Romantik”, appeared in 2004. Kontrast signed to Danse Macabre Records for 2008’s “Vision und Tradition”, which reached the top 10 of the Deutsche Alternative Charts and number one on the German Electronic Web Charts; its single “Durchbruch” also topped the German Electronic Web Charts.

Katrin Möller, performing as Nebelgeist, appeared as a guest vocalist on Kontrast releases before joining full-time. The band’s fourth album, “Balance” (2014), reached number three on the Deutsche Alternative Charts; its single “John Maynard”, a musical setting of Theodor Fontane’s ballad of the same name, reached the top five. A fifth album, “Unaufhaltsam”, followed in 2019 at number four on the Deutsche Alternative Charts. The current line-up is Roberto Lindner (vocals, lyrics), Dirk Heinrich (synthesizers, composition), Falko (synthesizers, mixing) and Nebelgeist (vocals).

Kontrast opened its sixth album as a two-part concept in 2025 with “Imperium – Tyrannis”, exploring a dystopian vision of a dictatorship that transforms people into dance machines. “Imperium – Proteus” completes the project through Danse Macabre Records, with both halves also combined on a single CD alongside separate digital and vinyl editions of each part.

items.title: Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits First Love in Video for “Hush Now” — “Trip” EP Out Now!
items.summary: Here we are again You look so familiar In this red light… Drop your mask, my friend Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and… The post Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits First Love in Video for “Hush Now” — “Trip” EP Out Now! appeared first
items.fullText:
Here we are again
You look so familiar
In this red light…
Drop your mask, my friend

Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and bring back every little thing you did to look at ease. You remember where you put your hands and the joke you made while you worked up the nerve to ask them to stay. The relief came when they heard the question in the joke and stayed a little longer. It can take years to realize how much you miss being known that well.

At the opening of “Hush Now (The Calling),” Apolonia sings to a familiar face bathed in red light, asking them to drop the mask with the gentle insistence of an old friend inviting you to sit and stay awhile. The track is the lead single from Trip, the four-track EP released November 20 by Hamburg noise-pop trio Seasurfer.

Christian Klepp’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.

Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels, then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours. On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track, One. The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless. The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.

 Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling), where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses. Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear”, where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

The drums make you wait for them again on “I See You”. The guitars pile up first, with the soft-edged distortion of Loveless, and the drum machine gives them a trip-hop lilt when it comes in. There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

Listen to Trip below and order the EP here.

items.title: BERMUD releases ‘Lost And Anxious’ single
items.summary: Montreal-based electronic shoegaze artist BERMUD released the single and video "Lost And Anxious" on November 20, 2026, ahead of the EP "Incoming Journeys."
items.fullText:
Montreal-based electronic shoegaze artist BERMUD released the single and video “Lost And Anxious” on November 20, 2026. The track is the lead single from the upcoming EP “Incoming Journeys,” due January 15, 2027 via We Are Not Alone Music and L’Autre Distribution, and is the second track on its tracklist.

BERMUD is the solo project of Elliot Aschard, originally from Angers, France, and now based in Montreal, Canada. “Lost And Anxious” pairs the project’s established shoegaze sound with 1990s-style techno beats, a shift from the material on BERMUD’s earlier releases. Aschard commented on the title: “I wanted to express the resilience with which we must face the world. […] We need connection and solidarity to keep from being pulled under by the turmoil. […] I’ve used a shoegaze aesthetic to bring us together, to foster a sense of unity in the face of events over which we have no control.”

About BERMUD

BERMUD is the solo project of Elliot Aschard, a shoegaze artist originally from Angers, France, who relocated to Montreal, Canada, in 2026. “Lost And Anxious” is the lead single from the project’s upcoming EP “Incoming Journeys,” set for release on January 15, 2027 via We Are Not Alone Music and L’Autre Distribution.

items.title: Instinct and Pain announce new album ‘Mauvaises Pensées’
items.summary: Sardinian gothic rock trio Instinct and Pain will release their second album "Mauvaises Pensées" on March 5, 2027 via Morella Records.
items.fullText:
Sardinian gothic rock and darkwave trio Instinct and Pain will release their second album, “Mauvaises Pensées,” on March 5, 2027 via Morella Records. Three singles lead up to the album: “The Death of Love” on December 4, 2026, “Poison Tree (A Garden of Silent Sins)” on January 8, 2027, and “Ashes of Light” on February 26, 2027, when album pre-orders also open on Bandcamp.

The ten-song record takes its title from a collection of thoughts by French poet and writer Paul Valéry, whose ideas inspired most of the songs. The band produced the album themselves, recording it with Salvatore Cabiddu at Tore Cabiddu Studio in Ghilarza and mixing and mastering it with Alberto Bandino at Cut Fire Mix Studio. The closing title track is an instrumental waltz featuring band family members as guests: Ethan Porcu on keyboards, Sara Manca on violin and Giulia Loi on clarinet.

“We would like people to hear our voice, what we feel through music, and the passion and commitment we put into making these songs,” said Alessandro Manca of Instinct and Pain.

Blake Carpenter, founder of Morella Records, described the band’s growth: “Instinct and Pain is a three-year-old band that sounds like they’ve been together for decades. The music is riveting, pure gothic post-punk, the vocals are brilliant and the musicianship is top notch. I’m honored to call Instinct and Pain a Morella family member.”

Tracklist

  1. Poison Tree (A Garden Of Silent Sins)
  2. The Death Of Love
  3. The Storm
  4. Ashes of Light
  5. Dust Claims All
  6. Over and Over
  7. Hope On a Tightrope
  8. Happiness With Closed Eyes
  9. I’m Nothing
  10. Mauvaises Pensées (instrumental)

Release schedule

  • December 4, 2026: “The Death of Love”
  • January 8, 2027: “Poison Tree (A Garden of Silent Sins)”
  • February 26, 2027: “Ashes of Light,” album pre-orders open on Bandcamp
  • March 5, 2027: “Mauvaises Pensées” album, on Bandcamp and streaming platforms

About Instinct and Pain

Instinct and Pain is a gothic rock and darkwave trio from Ghilarza, Sardinia, Italy, formed in 2023 by Alessandro Manca (vocals, guitar), Luca Porcu (bass) and Nicola Loi (drums). The band builds its songs on dark atmosphere and melancholic melody, with post-punk bones and a debt to the darker side of the 1980s underground.

Its debut album, “All Is Gone,” drew attention from the Italian press; critic Mick Mercer described the band as “vibrant Sardinian goth.” “Mauvaises Pensées,” the band’s second album, follows via Morella Records on March 5, 2027.

items.title: Night Nail releases ‘Feelings Are Monsters’ single and video
items.summary: Berlin darkwave act Night Nail released the single and video "Feelings Are Monsters" on November 20, 2026, the third single from "Infinite Fountain."
items.fullText:
Berlin darkwave act Night Nail released the single and video “Feelings Are Monsters” on November 20, 2026. The track is the third single from the band’s upcoming album “Infinite Fountain,” and is available as a digital single on Bandcamp.

Night Nail is the project of frontman Brandon Robert, who splits his creative base between Berlin and Los Angeles. Before starting the project, Robert worked as a hired-hand bassist in Hollywood. He has described a breaking point with a former bandmate who told him to “cheer up” during a period of depression: “I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again. I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you.”

Recommend to fans of Echo & the Bunnymen, The Cure and Clock DVA.

About Night Nail

Night Nail is a darkwave project founded by Brandon Robert around 2014, splitting its base between Berlin and Los Angeles. The band marked 10 years of its earliest recordings in July 2024 with “Early Demons & Demos 10th Anniversary Edition”.

The project first drew Side-Line’s attention in September 2023 with “Narcoleptic Dream Catcher”, the first single from an album released via Metropolis Records. “Fates Explained” followed as a video single that November, and in January 2024 the band released “Cracks In My Heart”, a video single featuring Luna De La Torre on vocals.

Night Nail’s sound draws on influences including Echo & the Bunnymen, The Comsat Angels, Trisomie 21, The Cult, The Sound, Christian Death, Wire, The Contortions, Clock DVA and The Cure. “Feelings Are Monsters” is the third single from the band’s upcoming album “Infinite Fountain.”

items.title: Conn.RAR releases EBM single ‘You Don’t Care’
items.summary: Conn.RAR has released the EBM single "You Don't Care" on Bandcamp and Spotify, written by founder Connor Eck after a corporate layoff.
items.fullText:
EBM act Conn.RAR released the single “You Don’t Care” on 20 November 2026, available on Bandcamp and Spotify.

The song addresses executive greed and the treatment of laid-off workers. Conn.RAR founder Connor Eck says the subject is a personal one: “We, the employees of the company I’d been working for were all educated, talented and had experience. But, despite all of that, we all got laid off when my employer was bought out.” Eck wrote, produced, mixed and mastered the track himself.

“You Don’t Care” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp and Spotify.

About Conn.RAR

Conn.RAR is the solo project of Connor Eck, who started out in 2020 making electronic music inspired by old video games and cyberpunk themes before shifting toward the hard, punchy EBM sound of acts like Front 242, A Split-Second and a;GRUMH. “You Don’t Care” is Conn.RAR’s latest single, built around Eck’s own experience of a corporate layoff.

items.title: Pawn Pawn releases synthpop single ‘Silhouette’
items.summary: Pawn Pawn has released the synthpop single "Silhouette," the first taste of the Toledo, Ohio trio's upcoming album "Thunder," due in early 2027.
items.fullText:
Synthpop trio Pawn Pawn released the single “Silhouette” on 20 November 2026, the first taste of the Toledo, Ohio band’s upcoming album “Thunder,” due in early 2027.

“Silhouette” pairs driving guitars with synth bass over a programmed beat. Lyrically, the song addresses the gap between a person’s unfiltered self and the version expected to be shown in public, where vulnerability is the price of being fully seen.

Liz Owens Boltz handles lead and backing vocals and wrote the lyrics. David Daniel Smith plays percussion and keys and adds backing vocals, while Brandon William Boltz plays guitar and backing vocals. The track was recorded by Brandon W. Boltz and David D. Smith at NoFocus Records and produced by the band, with mixing and mastering by Brett Dennison at FireFly Studios. Cover art is by CatBot Industries.

“Silhouette” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp and Spotify.

About Pawn Pawn

Pawn Pawn is a synthpop trio from Toledo, Ohio, combining rhythmic energy and dark soundscapes with subtle industrial-pop elements. The band has played live original music in Northwest Ohio since 2018 and headlined the Toledo Pride Kick-off Party in 2026. Side-Line previously streamed the band’s “Halloween” EP exclusively ahead of its release in January 2025. “Silhouette” is the band’s latest single and the first song revealed from “Thunder,” the album Pawn Pawn has set for an early 2027 release.

items.title: Laibach release ‘MUSICK : ENCORE’, a companion piece to ‘MUSICK’
items.summary: Laibach release 'MUSICK : ENCORE' on Mute, a companion album to 'MUSICK' with unreleased tracks and remixes by Richard X and Fat White Family.

Slovenian industrial collective Laibach release ‘MUSICK : ENCORE’ today via Mute, following the album’s announcement in September and an October preview single. The album gathers unreleased material from the “MUSICK” sessions alongside new remixes from Fat White Family & DJ Schopenhauer, Richard X, SILVERWINGKILLER, PUNCHBAG and others, extending the pop-leaning direction of Laibach’s 2026 album “MUSICK”.

“MUSICK : ENCORE”‘” is released as a 10-track vinyl edition, with four additional tracks exclusive to the CD and digital versions. The guest list spans several scenes: Fat White Family & DJ Schopenhauer remix “Fluid Emancipation”, Kaja Skrbinšek features on “This Is The End”, Senidah lends vocals to “Love Machine” (remixed by PUNCHBAG and separately by The Lincolnshire Poacher), and electropop producer Richard X co-produced several tracks and remixes “Resistencia”. Ghanaian artist Wiyaala features on two versions of “Musick”, Marina Mårtensson returns on “#US” (remixed by SILVERWINGKILLER) and “Faith No More”, and Manca Trampuš of Koala Voice and Bojan Cvjetićanin of Joker Out each guest on new tracks.

“Faith No More”, featuring Marina Mårtensson and Bojan Cvjetićanin, carries the official video embedded above.

About Laibach

Laibach formed in 1980 in Trbovlje, Slovenia, taking its name from the German name for Ljubljana under Habsburg and Nazi occupation. The group became the musical wing of the Neue Slowenische Kunst art collective, built around a confrontational aesthetic that reworks totalitarian imagery, military iconography and mass-culture symbols into statements whose political meaning stays ambiguous. Laibach signed to Mute in the UK during the 1980s and built a catalogue of reinterpretations alongside original material, including the 1987 album “Opus Dei” and its cover of Queen’s “One Vision”.

Across more than four decades, Laibach has continued to reinterpret other artists’ work as a core part of its method, from “Wat” (2003) through recent singles covering Foreigner’s “I Want To Know What Love Is”, Billie Holiday’s “Strange Fruit” and a tribute album of Rammstein covers. The band’s live work has ranged from a 2015 concert in Pyongyang, North Korea, to the large-scale symphonic project “Alamut” with A/Political in 2025.

In 2026, Laibach moved toward a more direct pop sound on the album “MUSICK”, built around high-concept electropop production and features from pop, electronic and underground guests across several countries. “MUSICK : ENCORE” extends that album with its outtakes and remixes, alongside the band’s continuing European tour dates into 2027.

items.title: Then Comes Silence split ‘Requiem Ballroom’ into two halves for eighth album
items.summary: Then Comes Silence release eighth album "Requiem Ballroom" on Metropolis Records, led by focus track "Witches and Demons", ahead of a January 2027 EU tour.
items.fullText:
Stockholm post-punk trio Then Comes Silence release their eighth album, ‘Requiem Ballroom’, on Metropolis Records, led by focus track ‘Witches and Demons’. Side-Line reported the album’s announcement in October; the 12-track album splits into two six-track halves, “Requiem” and “Ballroom,” each mixed separately around a theme of polarity.

Jon Bordon (Nicole Sabouné, Melody Club, The Exploding Boy) mixed the “Ballroom” half and Tom van Heesch (Rammstein, Apocalyptica, Backyard Babies) mixed the “Requiem” half. Svante Forsbäck handled mastering. Vocalist-bassist Alex Svenson produced the album and wrote all the lyrics and music. Drummer Jonas Fransson and guitarist Hugo Zombie complete the trio. Agent Side Grinder‘s Johan Lange adds synthesizer on the closing track.

“Since the album is divided into two halves, it’s important to give each part its own sound. It carries its own identity and the context is somewhat varied. That’s why we have two mixing producers, Tom van Heesch and Jon Bordon, each of whom takes care of one half. This album is simultaneously a game, a social experiment playing with polarisation. You pick one team. You can’t have both sides. Choose Requiem or Ballroom,” says Alex Svenson.

‘Requiem Ballroom’ follows the singles ‘Judgement Day’, ‘Remaker Redeemer’ and ‘Bye Bye Land’, released ahead of the album.

items.summary: And One release their 2003 album "Aggressor" on streaming services for the first time, out now via Out Of Line Music, with three more reissues to follow.
items.fullText:
Berlin synthpop and EBM group And One released their 2003 album “Aggressor” on streaming services for the first time on 20 November 2026, via Out Of Line Music. It is the first of four classic And One albums the label is bringing to streaming this winter.

“Aggressor” is sung entirely in German and was produced, arranged and mixed by frontman Steve Naghavi. “Krieger” was the album’s only single and remains a fan favourite, alongside “Schwarz” and “Fernsehapparat.” Across twelve tracks, the album pairs the band’s EBM roots with its synthpop hooks.

The “Aggressor” tracklist is: “Kein Anfang,” “Schwarz,” “Krieger,” “Sternradio,” “Speicherbar,” “Fehlschlag,” “Für Immer,” “Einstieg,” “Strafbomber,” “Fernsehapparat,” “Tote Tulpen” and “Kein Ende.”

The release opens a four-part digital roll-out of And One’s back catalogue on a biweekly schedule: “Nordhausen” (1997) follows on 4 December, led by “Sweety Sweety,” “Sometimes” and “Movie Star.” “9.9.99 9 Uhr” (1998) arrives on 18 December, headed by “Get You Closer,” “Pimmelmann” and “Love & Fingers.” “Virgin Superstar” (2000) closes the series on 31 December with “Panzermensch,” “Virgin Superstar” and “Goodbye Germany.”

In spring 2027, And One return to clubs with the “Bägtuse Ruts Tour,” a 31-date run through Germany centered on the band’s 1991-1998 material alongside new songs.

items.summary: Some Days Are Darker release "Playing With Fire," from the New York trio's album "Black Box Warning," out 13 November 2026 via Bandcamp.
items.fullText:
New York goth and synth-driven alternative rock trio Some Days Are Darker released the single and video “Playing With Fire” on 13 November 2026, taken from their album “Black Box Warning.” The twelve-track record was recorded with David Catching at Rancho De La Luna in Joshua Tree, California.

“Playing With Fire” follows the band’s September single “NDRI,” also pulled from “Black Box Warning,” which Side-Line covered on its release.

“Black Box Warning” was written by Lear Mason, except “Devotion” and “Playing With Fire,” co-written with drummer Robbie Williamson. The album was engineered by John Russo, produced by Mason and Williamson, mixed at Orange Blossom Studio in Phoenix, Arizona by Williamson, and mastered at The Loft Studio in Los Angeles. Bassist and keyboardist Chris Martin also plays acoustic guitar and mellotron across the record.

“Black Box Warning” is also available on Spotify and Apple Music.

About Some Days Are Darker

Some Days Are Darker began as the solitary songwriting project of former metalcore guitarist Lear Mason before growing into a three-piece with bassist, guitarist and keyboardist Chris Martin and drummer, multi-instrumentalist and producer Robbie Williamson. The band is based in New York.

Formed in 2019, the group released its self-titled debut album in 2022 and has shared stages with The Chameleons, Vision Video and House of Harm. They have toured the US East Coast and Canada with Pink Turns Blue and the US West Coast with Theater of Hate, with further East Coast dates planned around the release of “Black Box Warning.”

The band’s September single “NDRI,” also from “Black Box Warning,” was covered by Side-Line on its release. “Playing With Fire” is the second advance single from the same album.

items.title: Test Dept and Brith Gof share ‘Truan Yw Gennyf Fi / Lament’ single
items.summary: Test Dept and Brith Gof release 'Truan Yw Gennyf Fi / Lament', the third single from 'Gododdin: 2026 Remaster', out 4 December via Artoffact Records.
items.fullText:
London industrial group Test Dept and Welsh theatre company Brith Gof released the single “Truan Yw Gennyf Fi / Lament (Live in Polverigi 1989, 2026 Remaster)” on 20 November 2026 via Artoffact Records. It is the third advance single from “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster,” a 3CD/1DVD box set expanding the pair’s 1989 album “Gododdin,” due 4 December 2026.

The single is accompanied by a video assembled from footage of a 1989 live performance in a quarry in Polverigi, Italy, with the audio of the full show appearing on the third disc of the reissue. It follows two earlier advance singles from the same campaign: “Gwr A Aeth Gatraeth / Prologue (Early Studio Sessions, Reworked 2026)” and “Arddylegog Ganu / Heroic Society (Early Studio Sessions, Reworked 2026)”.

“We were physical performers as well as musicians in the live show, and in the aftermath of the battle we lay prostrate, exhausted in the mud of the flooded quarry as the bagpipes struck up heralding the lament for the fallen warriors,” says Test Dept’s Paul Jamrozy. “I had actually been a split second away from being a real fatality myself when a burning battering ram log broke free, hurtling down and crashing into the huge metal tank beside my head.”

“It was thrilling to be a part of this event, singing the ancient words of the poet Aneirin to music by Test Dept and John E R Hardy,” adds Brith Gof’s Lis Hughes Jones. “I looked out over the vast expanse of the sand quarry where a stunned audience stood as witnesses to the aftermath of battle. As the song came to an end the mournful sound of bagpipes took up the lament for the fallen.”

“Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” widens the original seven-track album with 19 previously unreleased recordings, for a total of 26 tracks across three CDs. The set includes a reworked perspective on the original release, drawn from multitrack tapes of early studio recordings, alongside the third disc capturing the 1989 Polverigi performance in full. A DVD carries a contemporaneous documentary combining live footage with interviews. All audio was remastered by Paul Lavigne at Kontrast Mastering. The reissue is packaged in a 5-panel ecopak with a 24-page booklet containing archival imagery and an essay by author Alexei Monroe. A separate red vinyl LP carries the original album with one previously unreleased track. Artwork for both formats comes from Paul Jamrozy and Stefan Alt (ant-zen).

The original “Gododdin” was produced by Ken Thomas at Jacobs Studios, built from Test Dept’s existing studio and field recordings augmented with brass and wind courtesy of Brith Gof’s John E R Hardy and bagpipes from Alistair Adams, with Jamrozy’s vocals set alongside Welsh-language vocals from Lis Hughes Jones. The piece is based on Y Gododdin, the earliest surviving Welsh-language poem, written around 600 AD, which tells of 300 Celtic warriors who attacked 100,000 invading Angles and lost. Test Dept and Brith Gof first staged it live at an abandoned Rover car factory in Cardiff in December 1988, with further performances in 1989 in Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” is the second entry in a series of Test Dept archival reissues, following the 4xCD “Industrial Overture. Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985” roughly a year earlier.

Test Dept have the following live shows confirmed:

  • 28 November 2026, Porto, Portugal, Auditório CCOP
  • 1-4 July 2027, Canterbury, UK, Shadowlands Festival

About Test Dept and Brith Gof

Test Dept formed in London in the early 1980s around Graham Cunnington and Paul Jamrozy, building an industrial sound from scrap metal percussion, factory tools and found objects alongside electronics, aligned with the miners’ strikes and labour politics of the era. Brith Gof is a Welsh avant-garde theatre company co-founded by Mike Pearson, known for large-scale, site-specific performance work staged in disused industrial buildings and open landscapes across Wales.

The two groups collaborated on “Gododdin,” a studio album and accompanying performance piece centered on the Welsh poem Y Gododdin, first staged at a derelict car factory in Cardiff in December 1988 with Lis Hughes Jones and John E R Hardy of Brith Gof joining Test Dept on stage. The production toured Italy, the Netherlands, West Germany and Scotland through 1989, including the Polverigi quarry performance captured on the current reissue’s third disc.

Test Dept signed to Artoffact Records in 2025 for a series of catalogue reissues and new material, beginning with the 4xCD “Industrial Overture. Studio & Live Recordings 1982-1985”. “Gododdin: 2026 Remaster” follows as the second release in that campaign, preceded by advance singles “Gwr A Aeth Gatraeth / Prologue” and “Arddylegog Ganu / Heroic Society,” with the full 3CD/1DVD box set due 4 December 2026.

items.title: “Forever in the Blood Moon” — Berlin Darkwavers Night Nail Head Out on a Ghoulish Commute in Video for “Feelings Are Monsters”
items.summary: Thoughts of dread for the living. Pandering with the queen of sorrow. Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow. Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such… The post “Forever in the Blood Moon” — Berlin Darkwavers Night Nail Head Out on a Ghoulish C
items.fullText:
Thoughts of dread for the living.

Pandering with the queen of sorrow.

Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.

Watch the video for “Feelings Are Monsters” below.

Night Nail formed in Los Angeles in 2013 and moved to Berlin before releasing their 2018 debut, LA Demons, on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed on Cold Transmission in 2020, and Metropolis released Fates Explained in 2023. William Faith and Sven Wolff handled mixing and post-production on Night Nail’s fourth studio album, Infinite Fountain. Wolff worked on “Feelings Are Monsters” at Berlin’s Cosmonaut Studio, with Night Nail co-producing and Alex Lee contributing additional synths.

Infinite Fountain was released on November 6, 2026, on Icy Cold Records, and the vinyl edition follows on December 4. Listen below and order the album here

items.title: Seattle Dungeon Synthpop Project PROFIT PRISON Asks What the Living Owe the Dead in Video for “In Memoriam”
items.summary: Their lives felt somewhat sound Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town and I loathe to tell you how it ends so in silence we bow our… The post Seattle Dungeon Synthpop Project PROFIT PRISON Asks What the Living Owe the Dead in Video for “In
items.fullText:
Their lives felt somewhat sound
Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town
and I loathe to tell you how it ends
so in silence we bow our heads

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen?, sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

items.fullText:
At the edge of the abyss I stand
Into the depths I am drawn
The future without me
Troglobite in bizarre light.

A red light in a fog-filled nightclub lets you see who’s beside you on the dance floor. In a limestone cave, a lamp can reveal an olm, a pale salamander that lives underground. For Hanover-based “singer-doomwriter” David Barteczko, who first played as KOSMOBERKH on an open stage in Oldenburg, there’s a kinship between those two kinds of light. He puts them side by side on Troglobiten in Absonderlicht, a title he translates as “Troglobites in Secluded Light.”

Released November 6, 2026, on Barteczko’s own Zeichenlos Records, the ten-track album is his first since 2018’s oneiroi, which came out under the name Mosaikh. A club gives young people somewhere to make things together and try out how they want to live. Barteczko’s characters are looking for that kind of room under political and economic pressure. Pandemic isolation, war, a changing climate and the lure of conspiracy theories and parallel lives online form the backdrop to the album’s loosely connected episodes.

That first stage was Craftwork Café at Oldenburg’s Metro discotheque, where Barteczko tried out songs between 2011 and 2013. He describes those sets in terms of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring and Joy Division’s “Dead Souls,” both evoked by a single acoustic guitar. The 2014 demo Urbild began his recording partnership with Alex Pojda. Barteczko set his voice aside for the instrumental post-rock of Dim Nachttag in 2016 and took up singing again with Mosaikh, the electric trio whose songs about belonging drew on his experience as a Polish migrant.

During the break from KOSMOBERKH, Barteczko played in prog-doom band CMDR RIKR and post-rock group BRUECKEN. He returned to the stage in May 2024, opening for Extra Life at Cadillac in Oldenburg with cellist Jann Michael Engel, whose credits include Anne Clark and Mila Mar. The pair recorded the cello in Göttingen, and Barteczko tracked his vocals, synths, percussion and effects at home. Most of the guitars were recorded at Holodeck Studio, where Pojda co-produced the album with Barteczko and mixed and mastered it.

Barteczko’s acoustic guitar and Engel’s cello are at the center of the record. Synths, electronic percussion and field recordings carry the arrangements into ethereal wave and chamber doom. Barteczko’s reference points range from early Dead Can Dance and Scott Walker’s Scott 4 to David Bowie’s The Man Who Sold the World and Peter Hammill’s In Camera.

Deep strums and a low cello line set the instrumental “Fiz Oblon” in motion. The opener, issued October 16 as the fourth and final advance single, has the pace of a walk by lantern light, with the drums moving steadily beneath the acoustic riffs and Alex Pojda’s bass carrying the rounded weight of gothic rock. Engel takes the cello higher against the guitar before a rubbery industrial darkwave beat takes over for a spell. The cello returns to pick up the melody. The piece is named for the Bippen discotheque where Barteczko developed his taste in music, and he dedicates it to the memory of Pai and Hage. In the single notes, he credits clubs like this one with bringing him to music and to people who stayed in his life.

Barteczko first sings on “Asche meiner Jugend,” in a high, unhurried voice over gentle acoustic guitar. The lyric puts crimson clouds in a skylight and stroboscopes in a room he once knew. He can picture it well enough to feel like a stranger there now. Reverb carries off the ends of his phrases in the chorus, and Engel comes in with a low, grieving cello line. The two instruments find a brisk folk rhythm as Barteczko sings with more force. The quicker rhythm gives him a few bars to dance on the ashes of his youth and ask if anyone can see him glow.

A light chime moves through “Sterngeworden” like bells attached to someone’s dancing feet. The acoustic guitar makes room for clear electric notes to ring, and Engel draws out one of his loveliest melodies. Barteczko’s languid delivery suggests The Replacements and The Cure. The acoustic playing has the intimacy of Nick Drake, and the electric guitar has the soft focus of dream pop. The singer looks to the past for some sense of what lies ahead. In the last lines, he hopes someone else’s longing might carry him home.

Getting home grows complicated on “Zugvogel.” Strings ripple behind the gentle acoustic strum while the cello keeps chugging along, and an electric-sounding quiver unsettles the edges of the arrangement. There’s something of The Cure’s “Catch” in the voice and the acoustic swing, set in a scene that could belong to a David Lynch film. One migrating bird loses its sense of day, night and direction. A second bird’s plumage is a business suit, and its days are a funeral procession. Those small, birdlike sounds leave the flight feeling as though it could take you from one dream, or one life, straight into the next.

There’s a dry click at the end of the guitar strokes in “Hybris.” Barteczko comes in slowly above a deep cello tone, with the deliberate phrasing of someone waking up and deciding he wants out. A brighter melody suddenly picks up the pace, then the playing shifts again into a loose, almost jazzy groove. Earlier figures reappear as quickly as the moods that brought them on. The words make a similar series of turns. One person wants to break free of himself, asks someone else to break free with him, and shudders when the thing they’ve made together breaks free in turn.

The acoustic strum on “Telegramme” sways as though it could stop between strokes, and there’s an ease to Barteczko’s delivery even as he sings about messages falling like ash and people being made to whisper obediently. Christoffer Grunau plays drums, and Udo Kirfel contributes bass. Engel holds a low, steady line before reaching up to accent individual phrases. His playing grows more melodic and climbs higher as the song closes. By then Barteczko is moving between a whisper and a shout, asking the other person to hold his hand and bracing himself for their answer.

The first single, “Stummfilm” (August 14), begins with a cello melody that nearly waltzes, the acoustic guitar keeping step. The introductory figure gives way to a gentler strum, and then the cello bears down again beneath Barteczko’s voice. In the lyric, two lives are bound up in a shared manuscript. He dips the other person’s page in ink, the paper tears, and he plays the images back in his head in silence. Guitar and cello build around him until his voice recedes. Engel takes the melody back with a little more lift to it, and the guitar falls in beside him.

The video reworks F. W. Murnau’s 1926 silent film Faust, bringing the outsized gestures of German Expressionism to the guilt and private fantasies of a relationship that has run out of words.

The second single, “Zypressen” (September 4), starts with a soft strum, a passing synth tone, and an especially tender vocal. Engel takes his time entering. Once he does, the cello zigzags across the guitar part and elaborates on its own melody while the singing pauses. The bow moves faster, and the synth tones darken. When the cello drops away, the voice and guitar briefly have the space to themselves. Engel comes back to carry the melody under the singing, and rain enters over gentle strumming. The close brings distorted electric guitar alongside the cello, and Barteczko’s voice sounds much farther away.

The song follows an exhausted nurse through an understaffed hospital ward, where she tends to cypresses in place of patients. The applause that keeps her awake at home recalls the people who took to their windows to clap for hospital staff during the pandemic. For the video, original art sits alongside paintings, notably the work of Swiss Symbolist Arnold Böcklin, whose cypresses take on an uneasy motion.

The instrumental “Oras Bad” opens with a rush of sound and a chime-like jangle. A soft, guitar-like figure trails into reverb above a low electronic hum. As the rush grows louder, that low tone holds its place with the clarity of one detail in a dream. Ora’s name returns when Barteczko calls for rain on the closing track.

Christof Schlaak’s high piano notes fall far apart in “Petrichor,” the album closer and third single, released September 25. They land like the first drops of rain on stone, with a soft acoustic strum underneath. Engel’s cello falls into step with Barteczko’s aching vocal for a few bars, then moves off on its own. When the electric guitar swells, the space between those sparse notes fills up with cello and piano over Grunau’s drums and Kirfel’s bass. The arrangement feels poised for a downpour. It ends with the electric guitar easing off into something close to a sigh.

Barteczko had planned to end the record with an instrumental until, as he recalls, “the first line escaped my lips.” The person singing it stands at the edge of an abyss, imagining a future that will go on without him. Then he catches the scent of rain. After an album full of people straining to get a word through, “Do you smell the rain?” is a question anyone standing beside him could answer.

The black gatefold vinyl is limited to 120 copies, and both the LP and the digital download are exclusive to Bandcamp. The album is also available on streaming services, including Spotify.

items.title: Ontario’s Fear Maintenance Pushes Joy Division’s “New Dawn Fades” to its Breaking Point
items.summary: Different colours, different shades Over each, mistakes were made I took the blame A change of scene can feel like a fresh start until you catch yourself having the same… The post Ontario’s Fear Maintenance Pushes Joy Division’s “New Dawn Fades” to its Breakin
items.fullText:
Different colours, different shades
Over each, mistakes were made
I took the blame

A change of scene can feel like a fresh start until you catch yourself having the same argument in a different room. Ian Curtis opens Joy Division’s “New Dawn Fades” with a tidy list of changes, delivered with the composure of somebody who might actually manage to make them. Then somebody raises their voice, somebody cries, and a man who says he’s walked on water and run through fire can barely feel a thing. The person he’s been waiting for turns out to be himself, and by then the promise of a new dawn has shrunk to “hoping for something else.”

On Unknown Pleasures, those are the last words you hear before you have to turn the record over. “New Dawn Fades” is track five, closing the side marked “Outside.” Factory Records released Joy Division’s debut in June 1979, following sessions with Martin Hannett at Strawberry Studios in Stockport. Peter Hook’s bass line sinks as Bernard Sumner’s guitar climbs, and Curtis’s voice grows increasingly unsteady between them. When he falls silent, the guitars play on for another minute, giving you time to sit with what he’s said before “She’s Lost Control” starts on side two.

In 1995, an instrumental edit of Moby’s cover brought that unease into Michael Mann’s Heat, where it plays over Al Pacino’s freeway pursuit. The song can keep you on edge with the words gone altogether. For Burlington, Ontario, musician Colin Adams, that possibility lay in the last minute of the original. He wanted to hear what would happen if the music went on gathering force after Curtis’s last line.

Adams explains, “You can feel the emotion building in the original recording with Ian Curtis pouring his soul out, but after the vocals end the intensity of the music gradually fades giving it a feeling of resignation. So, for this cover, I wanted to explore an alternate path and use that emotional intensity as a launchpad for a sonic explosion. In particular, with all the self-loathing lyrical content, I wanted to sonically explore the sound of someone in the midst of an emotional breakdown, with all the internal confusion, struggle and pain that could come with such an experience.”

Over four months in his Burlington home studio, Adams arranged and performed the cover and handled the production, recording, mixing, and mastering himself. He makes the coda the point where the music sounds closest to coming apart.

“New Dawn Fades” came out on November 18 as the third single from Fear Maintenance. Listen to the song on Spotify here.

For the video, Adams gave that breakdown a room of its own. He conceived, shot, and edited the clip himself at home, spending another four months working with a green screen and basic lighting in a ten-by-eight-foot space in his basement. He usually shot between ten at night and two in the morning.

Adams says, “The approach for the video was to reflect the internal strife and self-loathing of the protagonist as he metaphorically beat himself up.” Watch on YouTube.

For Adams, covering Joy Division began as a way to say goodbye to a former bandmate. He was fifteen when he joined the Toronto band Face of Another as its guitarist in 1986. Their bassist, Tim Smith, introduced him to Joy Division. The two fell out and never spoke again. After Smith’s sudden death decades later, the former bandmates revisited their old songs to give his family a record of that part of his life. On the second anniversary of Smith’s death, Adams recorded “Ceremony,” going back to the band Smith had put on for him all those years earlier.

The recordings that followed “Ceremony” gave Adams a way to “simultaneously pay homage to and reimagine some of the darker iconic songs from the post-punk bands of the late 1970s and 1980s” that inspired him to become a musician. He called the project Fear Maintenance after the label that released I Live, the 1995 EP by his second Toronto band, In Faith. The group played Toronto clubs from 1990 to 1995, often at Lee’s Palace.

Adams began putting the covers out as singles with Depeche Mode’s “Stripped” in December 2025 and then went to the other side of Unknown Pleasures for “Shadowplay.” For the next single, he returned to “New Dawn Fades,” which he’d recorded and filmed before he planned to put the covers on streaming services. The video had kept finding viewers in the meantime.

items.fullText:
Take my hand
And lead me home

Grief can make you very good at getting people to leave you alone. Say you’re getting by in a steady enough voice and even the people who know you best start to take you at your word. Then comes an evening when all you want to hear is somebody coming up the stairs.

Put that feeling on a record in 1988, and you might get New Edition’s “Can You Stand the Rain,” with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis leaving enough space around the beat for each voice to have its say. Sade’s “Love Is Stronger Than Pride” could lower the lights in a room just by coming on. At the last slow dance, a song like that bought you four minutes with your cheek against the padded shoulder of somebody’s jacket, trying to keep your white high-tops clear of their feet. Later, you might sit in the driveway with the engine off and the key turned just far enough to keep the late-night quiet-storm show on the radio.

At home, you could keep a blank VHS tape ready for the next time Donnie Simpson played your favorite video on BET’s Video Soul. The movies gave a record the hardest part of a conversation. Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark’s “If You Leave” scored the prom scene in Pretty in Pink. In 1989’s Say Anything…, John Cusack wore a trench coat over a Clash T-shirt and held a boombox over his head so Peter Gabriel’s “In Your Eyes” could reach a bedroom window.

Oakland, California quartet Still Ruins gives that difficult conversation the same room to breathe on “Armor Of Mourning,” the closing track of their debut LP, Through The Glass. Reverb stretches the opening drum hits, the synth bass ripples underneath, and a bright guitar part jangles into focus. The late-’80s R&B swing gives their mix of sophisti-pop, dream pop, and post-punk a slow dancer’s timing. Frankie Soto’s silky baritone holds the verse close before leaning into a melody big enough to follow somebody out of the theater.

At first he wants the door opened so people can see him on his way down. The blade in the refrain has gone weak and still cuts deep. Later, in the dark, he asks somebody to “share your grief,” offering the company he can barely admit he needs.

“As soon as we finished writing this song we knew it was going to be the final track on the record. We already wanted it to have a late 80’s RnB feel, something almost like Jam and Lewis could have written. Armor of Mourning starts off fairly emotional but by the end of the track it has the feeling of a final bow and the curtain closing: “Take my hand and lead me home.”

Eli Wengrin shot and edited the video, which looks exactly like it was captured during the period the band is trying to recreate with their sound. It encircles the band’s name with barbed wire before revealing the quartet on a wooden stage draped in black. The performance moves between warm hues and stark black-and-white close-ups, punctuated by glimpses of an overpass at dusk and an open book displaying plate armor. Beside the microphone, Soto extends an open palm, as though someone just beyond the frame might reach out and take his hand.

Watch the video for Armor of Mourning below:

Soto and multi-instrumentalist Jose Medina began writing together at a piano in Medina’s room. After years in the Central Valley DIY scene, they looked to Tears for Fears, R&B, and ’80s Spanish new wave for a different way to arrange their songs. Bassist Cyrus VandenBerghe helped turn the home-recording project into a live band, and keyboardist Marcos Gonzalez completed the quartet in 2025. They released their self-titled EP on Oakland’s Smoking Room and have shared bills with Provoker, House of Harm, and Johnny Dynamite.

Soto wrote lyrics by playing the instrumental demos and imagining what might have been happening onscreen. The quartet recorded Through The Glass at Medina’s home studio, building the arrangements with his collection of rackmount synths and digital effects. Claire Wardlaw plays saxophone over sequenced synths and 808 toms on the instrumental opener “Permanence.” Kurt Feldman of Ice Choir and The Pains of Being Pure at Heart mixed the album and contributed additional sequencing and backing vocals.

Through The Glass is out February 26, 2027, on Born Losers Records. Pre-order the album on Bandcamp or get the sea-blue vinyl from Born Losers Records.

items.fullText:
The struggle is real
but you know how it feels when you just don’t care

The world has developed a remarkable talent for turning misery into merchandise and selling rebellion back to the people it’s spent years beating into submission. Years of Denial have decided to dispense with the funeral arrangements and get the corpses dancing. Their latest album, Suicide Disco Vol. 3, offers twelve tracks of beautiful bad behaviour, political disgust, and the sort of bodily agitation that might alarm your physician.

Producer Jerome Tcherneyan pits deathrock guitars against militant EBM and electroclash’s synthetic vulgarity. Krautrock gives the arrangements a hard, even drive, while dub leaves enough room for the bass to throw its weight around. Somewhere between Chris & Cosey, Christian Death, and Public Enemy, the machinery develops a serious attitude problem.

In “Zero Fucks Given,” Barkosina Hanusova keeps coming back to “I started the fire,” shedding another reason to be careful with each pass. She’s got nothing to fear, nothing to lose, and nothing to hide. A stranger in somebody else’s “little town,” she calls herself a “weirdo” and sings “I am a cripple and a freak” with the relish of someone who knows the neighbours can hear her. “I am a misfit I live by it” makes a way of life out of a word meant to put her in her place.

The title refrain turns that declaration into a chant. The ending jams “kill society” and “kill me” into the same repeated line until “Why don’t you kill me” is all that’s left. Hanusova delivers the question like a dare to the people who have made her existence their business.

Director Simone Pellegrini gives that pressure a physical form. Hanusova performs amid broken plaster, fluorescent lights, and exposed cables while another woman strains against a leather straitjacket. The camera watches a corseted figure press her palms against scratched glass, giving you plenty of time to get uncomfortable on the other side of it.

Bathed in green light that highlights her fishnets, bandages, and knee brace, the corset-clad woman finally takes a crowbar to the room, prying it apart. The architecture has done plenty to earn it.

Watch the video for “Zero Fucks Given” below.

Tcherneyan was the drummer in Piano Magic before he and Hanusova started Years of Denial in 2016. The French producer and Czech vocalist build their live sets around hardware sequences and dub effects. Arpeggios lock into rhythms drawn from new beat and rave, and Hanusova brings her background in performance art to the stage, giving a gesture as much weight as a line.

Much of their catalogue took shape at Ark of Noise studio, with releases on Death & Leisure, Pinkman, and Veyl. Suicide Disco (2019) and Suicide Disco Vol. 2 (2023) established the series, and the remix EPs brought in Orphx, Silent Servant, and The Hacker. On 2025’s Love Cuts EP, Hanusova’s verses had to share the floor with drums that barely let up.

Across the new album, fury at a society that polices women’s bodies goes hand in hand with tenderness for the people on the receiving end. For anyone who’s ever been called the town freak, there’s company on this dance floor.

items.fullText:
In a crowded place I’m still unknown
Dancing lights, reflections in the night
Empty room just messes with my mind
The beat goes on

Modern civilization has become a magnificent assembly line of manufactured personalities, where everybody gets to be an individual provided they purchase the correct uniform, subscribe to the appropriate ideology, and maintain a sufficiently attractive digital representation of their miserable little existence. Meanwhile, the dancefloors are packed, the algorithms are thriving, and loneliness has apparently become humanity’s most reliable growth industry. Somewhere in this enormous psychological junkyard, Turkish post-punk duo Ductape have decided to examine the wreckage with their new album, Faded Flowers.

The title imagines humanity as a field of dying flowers, each individual slowly drained by repetition, conformity, and the exhausting business of pretending everything is perfectly wonderful. With fierce synthesizers, cold, commanding basslines, and Furkan’s wonderfully agitated guitar work, Ductape approach this collective nervous breakdown with considerable conviction. His guitar lines argue, interrupt, plead, and occasionally sound ready to file a formal complaint against the entire human race, while Çağla’s commanding vocals move between icy composure and emotional urgency.

D.E.R.T. carries these anxieties into a wonderfully strange visual territory. The video, filmed in grainy black-and-white by Begüm Koçum, moves between sunlit fields and stark portraits against a pitch-black backdrop. Elaborate clothing, sharply drawn makeup, and tightly framed gestures suggest a world where identity has become an elaborate theatrical production, complete with costumes, poses, and absolutely no guarantee that anyone knows their lines.

The lyrics address the absurd contradiction of feeling utterly alone in a room full of people. Music continues, bodies move, and everybody participates in the great social masquerade, yet genuine recognition remains frustratingly elusive. Beneath the insistent beat lies an existential question about authenticity and what it actually means to feel alive.

Then comes the enormous, roughly textured white sphere, resembling a moon that somebody has stolen from the heavens and brought along for moral support. Passed between Çağla and Furkan, it becomes an enigmatic object of shared concern, affection, and possibly cosmic responsibility. Clasped hands, intertwined bodies, and an outstretched sleeve connecting the musicians introduce moments of genuine tenderness amid the visual austerity. These gestures suggest that intimacy might offer some resistance to the machinery of alienation.

Watch the video for D.E.R.T below:

Throughout Faded Flowers, the duo take aim at contemporary society’s collection of false gods: institutional authority, manufactured ideals, rigid expectations, and the digital identities we dutifully polish while our actual personalities quietly disintegrate. The rhythms maintain their relentless forward momentum, giving the album the peculiar sensation of dancing through a civilization that has apparently misplaced its operating instructions. With Faded Flowers, Ductape offer a beautifully bruised examination of contemporary existence, where humanity keeps dancing despite having precious little idea why, and the possibility of connection remains worth fighting for.

items.title: San Diego Post-Punk Duo Twin Ion Engine Explores Romance and Ruin on Third Album “(III) Midsummer Lover”

items.fullText:
Romance is a magnificent form of voluntary insanity, a condition in which otherwise sensible people surrender their dignity to somebody who might eventually leave them standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, contemplating the emotional significance of an unanswered text message. Love makes idiots of intellectuals, poets of drunks, and philosophers of people who previously struggled to articulate anything more complicated than their lunch order. Fortunately, popular music has spent the better part of a century documenting this widespread psychological malfunction, and San Diego’s TWIN ION ENGINE have arrived with another contribution to the grand catalogue of catastrophe.

Founded in 2020 as the solitary musical enterprise of Eddie Lopez, TWIN ION ENGINE have grown into a post-punk and darkwave duo whose third studio album, (III) Midsummer Lover, explores the complicated business of wanting somebody, losing somebody, and occasionally wondering why anybody bothers with emotional attachments when solitary confinement seems considerably less exhausting.

Lopez recorded and produced the album himself, bringing collaborators Jo Esq and Ghost Days into a project whose musical vocabulary draws upon the stern basslines of European post-punk, the mechanical momentum of darkwave, and the melodic instincts of early-2000s indie rock. The guitars carry a romantic tension reminiscent of Twin Tribes, Early Cure, and The Chameleons, while the bass recalls the relentless forward movement associated with Molchat Doma. There are traces of Lebanon Hanover in the restrained vocal delivery, though Lopez appears equally interested in the possibilities of a good hook, allowing melody to interfere with the business of being miserable. That combination makes considerable sense. After all, romantic desperation has always benefited from a decent rhythm section, particularly when the alternative involves sitting alone with your thoughts and discovering how extraordinarily unpleasant your own company can become.

The title itself suggests an affection for romance in all its irrational glory. Summer promises temporary freedom, spontaneous encounters, reckless decisions, and the outrageous possibility that another person might somehow make existence tolerable. The season eventually ends, of course, leaving everybody to negotiate whatever emotional wreckage remains.

For TWIN ION ENGINE, that dedication provides an appealing premise: romance as an act of cheerful self-destruction, with guitars and synthesizers accompanying every questionable decision. Midsummer Lover invites the romantically afflicted to recognize themselves in its central preoccupation, because whatever else civilization manages to accomplish, people will continue falling hopelessly in love and making spectacular fools of themselves.
